newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Rwandan refugees head home, allege atrocities.
newsitem.headline: Rwandan refugees head home, allege atrocities.

text.p: Thousands of Rwandan refugees streamed into Sake at the northern tip of Lake Kivu on Wednesday and some accused Hutu militiamen of atrocities.

Refugees arriving from the two camps of Katale and Kahindo, which emptied after Zairean rebel attacks last month, said Interahamwe militiamen killed a large number of refugees because they were afraid of losing the human shield protecting them.
"More than a thousand are arriving in Sake each hour from the direction of the Masisi," said a UNHCR official standing at the entrance to the town, counting them as they arrived.
"In between ten and one o'clock today we had 1,582 children, 919 women and 641 men coming in."

Meanwhile in Minova, 17 kms (10 miles) south of Sake, more than 15,000 Rwandan refugees from camps around Bukavu, south of the lake, remained blocked in a makeshift camp on the edge of the water, prevented from moving on by men who may have been members of the Hutu Interahamwe militias.
The refugees arriving in Sake came from the camps of Katale and Kahindo, north of the city of Goma, which were attacked by rebels late last month.

"I left Katale camp on the 31st of October," said Prosper Ndukireyimenze, from Ruhengeri, northern Rwanda. "Before we left the area around Katale, on the second day, the militias killed a huge group of people."
Other refugees from Katale arriving in Mugunga near Sake told a similar tale.
"On the second day of walking we had got outside of the camp, when the Interahamwe killed three or four thousand people, west of the camp," one refugee said.
The flow into Sake continued throughout the afternoon.

"They are in good shape," said Freddy Moakata, a doctor with local Zairean aid agency Equipe d'Urgence et Biodiversite (EUB), adding: "Considering that most of them have been walking for over a month through the Masisi."
Thirty trucks, 20 of them from Rwanda, waited to ferry refugees from Sake to the Rwandan border at Goma.
Other refugees said the column of people arriving stretched for several kilometres back into the hills of the Masisi.
Zairean rebels opened the road south to Minova for access to reporters and aid workers on Wednesday and a UNHCR mission drove south to try to estimate how many refugees were on the road.

Up to 600,000 refugees have returned home to Rwanda since mid-November. Aid agencies think as many again may still be in eastern Zaire. They left in 1994 after a Tutsi army overran the country following the genocide of Tutsis by Hutu extremists, including the Interahamwe militia.
More than 15,000 refugees had gathered on a bend in the road through Minova, and in a forest at the side of the lake.
Local Zairean people were selling food and supplies of wood by the road but refugees said they had no money to pay for it.
"I came from Kashusha camp on the second of November, near Bukavu," said Emmanuel Nyamahunga, 35, who said he was a member of the committee controlling the camp in Minova.
"The Zairean rebels have said that we cannot move further towards Sake because of insecurity on the road. We are dying here, we have no food, no water and no firewood," he said.

Rebel soldiers said the refugees were not being stopped from moving north. The threats and instructions from Nyamahunga and his colleagues seemed to be the main reasons why the refugees were not moving.
Nyamahunga said he was not going home to Rwanda.
"It is not that I don't want to, it's that I can't. I haven't killed people, but I know I will be treated as a killer," he said.

"But we are telling these people to stay here, not to move to Sake, and so they are doing as they are told," continued Nyamahunga. "When we get back to Rwanda, there will be a war much worse than the one in 1994."
